content.title: Response to R4
content.comment:
Thanks very much for your constructive comments. We clarify the contribution of this work and elaborate on the evaluation with same training corpus in W2 and W3.  


### Q1: The findings are already known.
There is a possible misunderstanding of the position of our paper. We clarify that our work is a systematic investigation which builds a comprehensive evaluation protocol for investigating the benefits of vision signals for language models, with CLIP as a representative. These findings are meaningful in two aspects:

1. As stated in Q3 in our general response, we perform a more rigorous evaluation in W1 and W2, which has not been done in previous studies and our results provide a more solid basis for those findings. 

2. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to probe the model performance regarding the embodied knowledge such as the temperature. The findings are interesting which reveal that vision signals are beneficial for learning this challenging knowledge, based on the difficulty of transferring knowledge in the visual world to embodied. 

We believe these findings are important and could potentially inspire future studies towards better improvements of language models, and designing multi-modal models. 


### Q2: Why don't you evaluate models trained from scratch in W2 and W3 tasks .

Thanks for your suggestion. We provide the corresponding results in Q1 of the general response. It can be found that the caption corpus improves BERT and GPT on the visual-related task, yet they still struggle when dealing with the embodied knowledge. This is consistent with findings in our main paper. Besides, our investigation on the original BERT and OPT models can be treated as an exploration to probe the emergent abilities of large scale language models. Our investigation has interesting findings: after pre-training on large-scale text corpus, OPT-175B exhibits strong color and material recognition performance. However, the embodied knowledge cannot be acquired via pure text based language modeling, indicating that the generalization from W2 to W3 is not trivial via simply text-only training data. On the contrary, the CLIP model with much fewer parameters can consistently perform well in W2 and W3, validating the effectiveness of visual signals. 


We hope that our response can resolve your concerns about the findings and the evaluation. 
We would appreciate it if you could reassess the paper, and discussions are always welcome, thank you!

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies whether the language encoder of CLIP, pre-trained on image-caption pairs, perform better on language-only tasks that tests 1) linguistic 2) visual and 3) embodied knowledge (e.g., whether water is colder than the frying oil or not). Compared to language models trained only on text corpora (e.g., OPT), they find that CLIP performs worse on 1 but better on 2 and 3.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pro: Prior work considers mostly linguistic and visual knowledge probing while this paper shows that CLIP also encodes certain embodied knowledge. 

---
Cons:

1. Vision supervision or text domain difference?

Why CLIP performs well on visual/embodied knowledge related questions? E.g., the water is colder than the frying oil. 

Two hypothesis could explain it:

H1. The model can learn it from pure text data if the corpora have a lot of sentences like “the frying oil is hot” and “the water is cold”.

H2. The model learns what is visually “hot” and “cold” and could thus learn “water is colder than the frying oil” through visual supervision.

Based on the title of the paper, the authors seem to suggest that H2 is the reason, by comparing CLIP to OPT. However, CLIP and OPT are trained on different text data; thus we cannot conclude the role visual supervision plays. A fair baseline to CLIP would be training a language model also on the caption data CLIP was trained on.

2. Findings similar to prior work

Two aspects (W1 and W2) investigated in the work have been thoroughly discussed in prior work. Given that CLIP does well on W2 (e.g., encoding color, shape, material, etc), I am not sure evaluation on 3 more dimension from W3 (mass, temperature, hardness) is that novel.

3. Different probing methods make the results less rigid

Probing methods are known to have high variance. The models (BERT, OPT, CLIP) are tested with different probing methods, which could make the results less rigid. Prior probing studies at least apply the same prompts to different models.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper presents some new findings, it does not provide deep insight into the role “visual supervision” plays in training language models. The models the authors compare are not very comparable given the different training data and probing methods, making it hard to draw a conclusion.

content.title: Response to R2
content.comment:
Thanks very much for you comments. Our responses for your questions are below.

### Q1: Vision supervision or text domain difference?

We verify this by providing results in W2 and W3 with models trained on the exactly same text corpus, i.e., YFCC15M dataset. Please check the Q1 in our general response for more details. 

### Q2: Findings are similar to prior work.

For the clarification on the novelty of findings in W1 and W2, please refer to Q2 in our main response. 

Besides, we argue that performing well in W2 does not guarantee satisfactory results in W3. For example, OPT models such as OPT-13B perform relatively well in some W2 tasks like color and material identification, However, they perform much worse on the embodied knowledge related tasks, achieving results close to random guessing performance. CLIP models, with the supervision from vision signals, consistently outperform textual-only counterparts in both W2 and W3. We believe that these results are interesting and the LiVE benchmark can facilitate future studies.


### Q3: Differences of prompting methods lead to less rigid results.

We design the prompting method to fit the pre-training objective of each model, which is vital for eliciting the knowledge from pre-trained language models. Besides, we determine specific prompts to different models according to our prior to fit the training data distribution, i.e., designing sentence-like prompts for BERT and OPT, and caption-like prompts for CLIP models. While performing poorly when evaluated in a zero-shot fashion, BERT performs much better  in W2 after fine-tuning, and the OPT-175B also benefits from the in-context demonstration with few examples represented in the prompt. Yet, they still perform much worse than the CLIP models, especially in W3. These results verify that the prompting methods can effectively elicit the corresponding knowledge, and justifying the effectiveness of visual signals improve the embodied knowledge learning of language models.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on understanding why V&L pretrained models perform not well on language understanding tasks when they perform really well on vision tasks. The authors examine the case of CLIP model by comparing it with baselines such as BERT in three different styles of benchmark (i) linguistic (probing syntactic and semantic knowledge) (ii) visual world, text tasks involving visual common sense (iii) embodied worled evaluating physical-related knowledge than can only be learnt through interaction. The authors find that although CLIP doesn't do well against the counterparts in the (i), it does outperform non-visual baselines in (ii) and (iii).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- Good analysis and motivation on understand if text encoder in the V&L models are any good.
- Introduces a benchmark with 3 categories to test the proficiency of the text encoder across linguistic, visual and physical reasoning.
- Provides comparisons with non-visual baselines and some variants of CLIP 
- Good qualitative analysis on the embodied knowledge in the visual representations that suggests that CLIP indeed captures some of the visual semantics.
- Human annotated comparisons to show that CLIP is indeed really good.

### Weaknesses
- The paper unfortunately currently ignores a long line of research work that has been specifically done on improving the text encoder in vision and language models. The SimVLM [1] first showed that with proper pretraining objective, a V&L model can also perform substantially on the NLU tasks. This paper also had a result for fine-tuned VisualBERT [2] which was actually doing quite well on the downstream tasks. UniT [3] was a single unified network that worked on all domains well. FLAVA [4] and Unified-IO [5] models focus on specifically making these models work on text tasks and have impressive performance. I would suggest that authors do a proper juxtaposition with these models and include them in the comparisons.
- The formulation of the zero-shot prompting for the visual and embodied knowledge tasks is different for CLIP and BERT and hence it is unclear on whether BERT is performing at the max level and if the comparison is actually fair. Furthermore, the almost random averages of any other model except CLIP on the embodied task is somewhat concerning. With few-shot as shown on page 7, the OPT model does indeed perform much better? Was the prompts for the language models fine-tuned in any way? It would be interesting to also see how a model like FLAVA which also has both better text and multimodal encoder performs on these tasks. See next comment on how to possibly alleviate this.
- For W2, BERT and RoBERTa on the same scale as OPT (125M) are random while OPT does have some good performance. This is somewhat concerning. The authors do mention that they tried other prompts for MLMs but it is unclear how much difference did that make. Is this result a shortcoming of the formulation of the problem. Have authors tried fine-tuning for few shots and see if it helps? For BERT and RoBERTa, similar to CLIP, the sentence embeddings can also be compared for cosine distance. cos(CLS for o1, CLS for a) compared with cos(CLS for o2, CLS for a).
- In Section 4.1, the paper cripples the BERT baseline by only training it on the text corpus which is just the captions from YFCC-15M dataset. How was Next Sentence Prediction applied here as most of the sentences in YFCC-15M are only single sentences? We know from models like Flamingo [6] if there is enough text structure to learn generation instead of just single sentence such as caption, the model can do well on Visual and Language tasks as well compared to CLIP as learning the long term temporal dependency is necessary for performing well on NLU tasks such as QA and others. If we take authors comparison head on, it would be good to have a baseline such as VILT [7] (DeCLIP is there but that is mixed signal) also trained on YFCC100M with a pure MLM objective to understand and disentangle how much of a difference does the pretraining objective make. 
- It is also unclear why do we think CLIP as a model will gain the knowledge about physical world while GPT-style model won't from the text. A case study has been done on CLIP's embeddings for a video but a similar setting hasn't been tested for language models when you use descriptions for the image as the input.

[1] Wang, Zirui, et al. "Simvlm: Simple visual language model pretraining with weak supervision." arXiv preprint arXiv:2108.10904 (2021).

[2] Li, Liunian Harold, et al. "Visualbert: A simple and performant baseline for vision and language." arXiv preprint arXiv:1908.03557 (2019).

[3] Hu, Ronghang et al. "Unit: Multimodal multitask learning with a unified transformer." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.

[4] Singh, Amanpreet, et al. "Flava: A foundational language and vision alignment model." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

[6] Alayrac, Jean-Baptiste, et al. "Flamingo: a visual language model for few-shot learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2204.14198 (2022).

[7] Kim, Wonjae, Bokyung Son, and Ildoo Kim. "Vilt: Vision-and-language transformer without convolution or region supervision." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.

- The authors make a claim that they don't use GLUE and other evaluation benchmarks to avoid the confounding effect of fine-tuning the language models on them in Section 2.1. Then, authors continue to do a zero-shot and edge probing evaluation for their tasks. Is there a particular reasons why authors didn't do zero-shot and similar evaluation on the main evaluation benchmarks as there is enough literature with baselines.

content.title: Response to R1
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your insightful comments.  For the weakness you mentioned, we hope the response below can help you to better reacess the paper.

### Q1: Discussion and comparison with other VLM variants.  
During the preparation of this work, we do have many choices as there are many VLMs studies for investigation. After careful examinations, our study finally chooses the text encoder in the CLIP for investigation mainly due to two reasons:

(1) As the evaluation is language-oriented, the evaluated models are supposed to be able to deal with inputs with pure text. For example, single stream VLMs such as Oscar that require inputs with images. The SimVLM alleviates this issue by introducing a PrefixLM objective, with support of pure text input. However, as the pre-training procedure requires the model to generate the captions conditioning on the images inputs, there is a clear gap between the evaluation with text only and the pre-training, which influences the zero-shot performance and thus make the comparison not fair as well.

(2) The CLIP text encoder only adopts the image-text matching objective for pre-training, ablating the effect of other objectives that might dilute the contribution of visual signals. For example, the text encoder in UniT adopts BERT weights for initialization and FLAVA’s text encoder is trained with a mixed objectives of vision signals and mask language modeling. Performing comparison with these models cannot provide sufficient evidence  to illustrate the answer of our questions.
Thanks again for providing these interesting studies, and we will discuss them in the related work section and try our best to evaluate these models in our revision. 

### Q2: Difference in Prompting Setup for different models.

Please see our Q2 in the general response for details.

### Q3: Fine-tuning results and sentence embedding for BERT.

We provide fine-tuning results in the Q2 of general response, where extra supervision helps yet the models still struggle in challenging W3 tasks. For the sentence embedding method, we note that it is not feasible in the zero-shot setting, as the vanilla [CLS] representation cannot provide meaningful sentence representations without fine-tuning. 

### Q3: Details of BERT pre-training and comparison with CLIP.

Thanks for your question. We clarify that in our BERT pre-training, we only adopt the Mask Language Modeling as the pre-training objective, and remove the Next Sentence Prediction objective as there many studies show that it contributes little to the pre-training (see RoBERTa paper for details). Therefore, the comparison between the BERT and CLIP is fair regarding the dataset and model architecture, and the performance difference can be attributed to the pre-training objective, which answers our question of what vision supervision brings to the language models.

### Q4: Why CLIP learns embodied knowledge?

Thanks for your question. Our main assumption is that the embodied knowledge from images can be propogated into the language models during the contrastive pre-training. We would like to dig into this in the future, for example, examining the hypothesis with more experiments and utilizing the learned embodied knowledge of CLIP to improve the performance of text-only PLMs.

content.title: Thanks for the rebuttal
content.comment:
I would like to thank the authors for their rebuttal. I have read their response and other reviews carefully. I would like to keep my rating as it is because most of my questions I believe are still unclear but are important in gauging the impact of this work.

- Fine-tuning on BERT: The authors provide results on few-shot tuned BERT model with PET objective but few-shot/zero-shot setups are not fair for the model trained with denoising objective as seen from T5 paper and a full finetuning should be performed. I am also not sure about the statement "or the sentence embedding method, we note that it is not feasible in the zero-shot setting, as the vanilla [CLS] representation cannot provide meaningful sentence representations without fine-tuning." I think doing the comparisons in a fair way is actually required to understand the gap. If [CLS] representation is used on both sides I believe it should achieve the same effect.

- Pretraining on YFCC15M: It is unclear if YFCC15M is the right dataset for pretraining with pure text MLM objective. This baseline would still be crippled because the captions are not very meaningful in a MLM setup. Take an example of a caption "A man is wearing a [MASK] colored shirt". In no way possible without extra context, the model will be able to learn this without visual information. This is overall an unfair setup for BERT baseline still.

- CLIP's embodied knowledge: This claim is central to the paper and as Reviewer PpQ8 noted this needs to be disentangled for better understanding of what is happening and in general I think the rebuttal doesn't resolve this.

I once again thank the authors for taking time to write the rebuttal and helping me in improving understanding of their paper.

content.title: General Responses to Common Questions
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions. We reply to the common questions as below, and give the individual answers for specific questions to each reviewer.

### Q1: Whether the text domain differences leads to the performance variations in visual world (W2) and embodied world (W3).

**Text domain differences are NOT the exact reason for performance variations in W2 and W3**. 

We provide the results in W2 and W3 of three models with the identical architectures trained on the same YFCC-15M corpus (see the following tables). The only difference is the pre-training objective, i.e., masked language modeling for BERT, causal language modeling for GPT and contrastive image-text matching for CLIP. We observe that the captions in YFCC-15M do improve the related visual-related abilities to some extent, yet the text-only models still struggle in the embodied world. 
On the contrary, CLIP still performs the best in both W2 and W3, for example, it significantly outperforms the GPT in W3 by an 12% absolute accuracy. These findings indicate that the text domain difference cannot fully explain the performance variations in W2 and W3, and again verify the effectiveness of visual signals that are beneficial for learning knowledge in the visual and embodied world, which is consistent with the conclusion in our main paper. 

Besides, the results in the main paper with original BERT, OPT and CLIP models are meaningful as well. As the ability of language models emerges as a combination of the model architecture, training datasets, and computation used[1], the original model maintains the characteristics of large-scale pre-training. Investigation into these models reveals that some visual tasks and embodied knowledge are still challenging for large language models with the current training recipe, opening research directions on the pre-training for better informing LM with knowledge beyond the textual world.

content.title: Q2 & Q3
content.comment:
### Q2: Different zero-shot prompting methods may lead to unfair comparison.
We design the prompting methods to best fit the pre-training objective of the language models, which has been reported to be very important to utilize the model ability acquired during the pre-training [2]. 
Besides, we manually write about 10 prompts using our prior (shown in Appendix)  for each model to report the average performance for the results. 
We did not do exhaustive search for the prompts as sensitivity to prompts also indicates the ability of LMs. If a language model performs worse under a large range of prompt pools,  it also can prove the low generalization LM ability.
Furthermore, the few-shot in-context demonstration results of OPT in Figure 3 shows that OPT-like models can learn some knowledge with demonstrated examples. 
We also add a few-shot fine-tuning experiment following PET[3] for vanilla BERT and RoBERTa on the most challenging W3 tasks, where the language model head is tuned using 16-shot examples.
We observe that the performance of masked language models improves after fine-tuning, yet the results are far still worse than CLIP models. These results verify that our setup is reasonable, i.e., the formulation can elicit the knowledge in the models, yet text-only models still perform poorly under zero-shot or few-shot learning compared with CLIP models.
Besides, base and large models obtain no significant difference results in W3 even after fine-tuning, while the large-sized models are usually reported with better results in NLU tasks [4,5]. This contradiction again indicates that the embodied knowledge cannot be learned by introducing more parameters, which is consistent with our findings on OPT series models. Therefore, we think that the current setup is fair and the clear performance gaps between the models are sufficient to draw the conclusions.

| BERT-base     | 64.72(4.77)  | 55.62 (1.34) | 51.80 (1.31) | 57.38 |
| BERT-Large    | 65.47 (4.86) | 54.19 (2.31) | 52.73 (1.22) | 57.46 |
| RoBERTa-base  | 60.24 (5.24) | 60.27 (4.85) | 50.44 (1.13) | 56.98 |
| RoBERTa-large | 61.18 (4.01) | 58.28 (2.09) | 50.56 (1.14) | 56.67 |





### Q3: On the novelty of findings in linguistic world (W1) and visual world (W2):

There is a potential misunderstanding of the motivation for our investigations in the linguistic world (W1) and the visual world (W2).  
We would like to clarify that we define and perform evaluation in these two world scopes for a comprehensive and systematic investigation regarding the core scientific question: what vision signals bring to the language model.
Although intuitive findings have been observed in previous studies, there are variations regarding the training corpus, language encoder architecture and initialization[6], which makes the comparison unfair and hard to draw solid conclusions. In our paper, **our NEW finding in W1 is that text-only LMs still perform better than CLIP under fair settings with the same setups**. The BERT, CLIP, DeCLIP models are pre-trained on the same YFCC-15M corpus using the same Transformer architecture and initialization seed, with the only difference on the pre-training objective, i.e, MLM for BERT and Contrastive Image-Text Matching for CLIP. 
This comparison is not evaluated by previous studies, and we believe that our conclusion in W1 is more solid due to the more fair setup. 

For the observation in W2, to the best of our knowledge, **it is the first evidence showing that scaling up text-only models can lead to a better zero-shot performance on visual-related tasks** such as color and material identifications than vision-aided models like CLIP. 
We also conduct human evaluation to better illustrate that OPT-175B and CLIP performs closely to humans on specific tasks.

In all, we believe that these findings contribute to strengthening our understanding of the question of what vision brings to language models.
